title: Wedge-tailed eagle modelling
text: This site collects the analysis notebooks for modelling the flight behaviour of GPS-tracked wedge-tailed eagles (Aquila audax fleayi) in Tasmania.

title: Wedge-tailed eagle modelling
text:
Behaviour classification

K-means Instantaneous Variable: using variables calculated for each GPS fix to estimate behavioural states.
K-means Aggregated Variables: using variables that aggregate over a moving window (such as cumulative turning angles or average speed) to estimate behavioural states. This approach helps to smooth over jumpy states when using k-means, which treats each each sample independently.
K-means Combined Variables: using both instantaneous and aggregated variables to estimate behavioural states.
Hidden Markov Model: using a Hidden Markov Model to estimate behavioural states based on the observed GPS data.
EMbC Aggregated Variables: using expectation-maximisation binary clustering (EMbC) on the absolute cumulative turning angle and mean vertical rate over a moving window, following Scacco et al. (2019). The vertical rate split is fixed at 0 to separate gliding from soaring and flapping, and the states are smoothed after classification.
Agreement Between Methods: comparing the states from the 3-state k-means and HMM classifications.

title: Wedge-tailed eagle modelling
text:
Modelling the energy landscape
Using the soaring behaviour identified by the classification methods to determine where wedge-tailed eagles ‘harvest’ environmental energy (uplift from thermals and wind deflected off terrain), and how this relates to landscape features.

Data

Soaring Bouts and Energy Harvesting Data: selecting the fixes that most of the classification methods agree are soaring (ascending), splitting them into soaring bouts, and summarising when and where the eagles soar and how much altitude they gain. This creates the data that will be used to associate soaring with landscape variables (such as elevation, topographic position and ridges), but doesn’t do the modelling itself.

title: Wedge-tailed eagle behavioural classification
text:
Create aggregated features
For each location (the focal fix) we summarise the flight variables over a centred moving window that extends half_window_s seconds before and after it, within the same flight segment. As the data are classified after the fact, a centred window avoids shifting the detected transitions later in time (as a backward-only window would). Windows are based on time rather than a number of fixes, as the fix-intervals vary (mostly 3–5 s).
Within each window we calculate:

turn_cum - the cumulative signed turning angle (radians). When thermalling the turns all have the same sign, so the sum grows steadily (roughly 2π per circle), whereas the GPS jitter of a perched or slow bird has a random sign and largely cancels out.
speed_mean - the mean ground speed (m/s, from F_Sn).
Vrate_mean - the mean signed vertical rate (m/s, from F_Vrate), i.e. the net climb or descent.
straightness - the net displacement across the window divided by the path length (0 = returning to the start, 1 = perfectly straight). This separates directional flight from circling, and complements turn_cum for perched/slow birds (low straightness but little net turning).
n_fixes - the number of fixes in the window. This is not for clustering, but shows where windows are truncated at the start and end of flight segments (or across gaps in the data).

The turning angle is taken from step_ta, which is in radians. The turning angle of the first fix of each flight segment is relative to a step outside that segment, so it is set to 0.
The windows are calculated after removing the extreme vertical rates (so they don’t contaminate the window means), but before the low-speed rows are dropped below. Where fixes are missing, straightness uses the straight line between the remaining fixes. Each column gets a _window suffix (e.g. F_turn_cum_window). The column names don’t depend on the window width, so half_window_s can be changed below and the rest of the notebook re-run without any other changes.


Show code
# half-width of the window in seconds (the window covers this many seconds
# before AND after the focal fix)
half_window_s <- 15

# sum of x across each window, using cumulative sums (fast on millions of rows).
# lo and hi are the indices of the first and last fixes in each window
window_sum <- function(x, lo, hi) {
  cs <- c(0, cumsum(x))
  cs[hi + 1] - cs[lo]
}

add_window_features <- function(data, half_window_s) {

  data %>%
    arrange(name, flight_n, stepend_dtime) %>%
    group_by(name, flight_n) %>%
    mutate(
      t = as.numeric(stepend_dtime),
      # first and last fixes within +/- half_window_s of each focal fix
      lo = findInterval(t - half_window_s, t, left.open = TRUE) + 1,
      hi = findInterval(t + half_window_s, t),
      n_fixes = hi - lo + 1,
      # turning angle (radians), ignoring the turn at the start of each flight segment
      ta = if_else(row_number() == 1, 0, step_ta),
      turn_cum = window_sum(ta, lo, hi),
      speed_mean = window_sum(F_Sn, lo, hi) / n_fixes,
      Vrate_mean = window_sum(F_Vrate, lo, hi) / n_fixes,
      # net displacement / path length, both from the positions of the fixes in the
      # window (so it stays <= 1 even when fixes have been filtered out). seg is the
      # distance from the previous fix, so the path in a window is the sum of
      # seg over fixes lo+1 to hi
      seg = c(0, sqrt(diff(stepend_utme)^2 + diff(stepend_utmn)^2)),
      path_length = window_sum(seg, lo, hi) - seg[lo],
      displacement = sqrt((stepend_utme[hi] - stepend_utme[lo])^2 +
                            (stepend_utmn[hi] - stepend_utmn[lo])^2),
      straightness = if_else(path_length > 0, displacement / path_length, 0),
      .after = F_radians_abs
    ) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(-c(t, lo, hi, ta, seg, path_length, displacement)) %>%
    rename_with(\(x) paste0("F_", x, "_window"),
                c(turn_cum, speed_mean, Vrate_mean, straightness)) %>%
    rename_with(\(x) paste0(x, "_window"), n_fixes)

}

title: Wedge-tailed eagle behavioural classification
text:
Label the states
The cluster (k-means) and state (HMM) numbers are arbitrary, so state 1 in one method isn’t necessarily state 1 in another. Here we assign the same behaviour labels that were given to the 3-state models in each of the classification scripts.
Note that these need to match the labels in the classification scripts - if the models are re-run and the numbers change, update them here as well.


Show code
# the names of the state columns, and labels to use in the plots
state_cols <- c("kmeans_inst", "kmeans_agg", "kmeans_comb", "hmm")

method_labels <- c(kmeans_inst = "K-means instantaneous",
                   kmeans_agg = "K-means aggregated",
                   kmeans_comb = "K-means combined",
                   hmm = "HMM instantaneous")

# colours that are used in all of the plots and the map
state_colours <- c(ascending = "#E69F00", flapping = "#56B4E9", gliding = "#009E73")

# the consensus state can also be 'no majority' (when fewer than 3 methods agree)
# consensus_colours <- c(state_colours, "no majority" = "#999999")
consensus_colours <- c(state_colours, "no majority" = "red")

agreement_colours <- c("all 4 agree" = "#0072B2",
                       "3 of 4 agree" = "#F0E442",
                       "no majority" = "#D55E00")

# the labels from each classification script
eagle_states <- eagle_states %>%
  mutate(
    
    kmeans_inst = case_when(kmeans_inst == 1 ~ "ascending",
                            kmeans_inst == 2 ~ "gliding",
                            kmeans_inst == 3 ~ "flapping"),
    
    kmeans_agg = case_when(kmeans_agg == 1 ~ "flapping",
                           kmeans_agg == 2 ~ "gliding",
                           kmeans_agg == 3 ~ "ascending"),
    
    kmeans_comb = case_when(kmeans_comb == 1 ~ "gliding",
                            kmeans_comb == 2 ~ "flapping",
                            kmeans_comb == 3 ~ "ascending"),
    
    hmm = case_when(hmm == 1 ~ "gliding",
                    hmm == 2 ~ "flapping",
                    hmm == 3 ~ "ascending")
    
    ) %>%
  # use the same factor levels for every method (so the colours are consistent)
  mutate(across(all_of(state_cols), \(x) factor(x, levels = names(state_colours))))

title: Wedge-tailed eagle behavioural classification
section: Calculate the agreement between the methods
text:
Calculate the agreement between the methods
For each fix we count how many of the four methods classified it as each state. From this we get:

n_agree - the number of methods that agree on the most common state (2, 3 or 4)
agreement - whether all 4 methods agree, 3 of the 4 agree, or there is no majority (a 2-2 or 2-1-1 split)
consensus - the state that at least 3 of the 4 methods agree on (otherwise ‘no majority’)
odd_one_out - when 3 of the 4 methods agree, the method that disagrees



Show code
eagle_states <- eagle_states %>%
  mutate(
    # the number of methods that classified each fix as each state
    n_ascending = rowSums(across(all_of(state_cols), \(x) x == "ascending")),
    n_flapping = rowSums(across(all_of(state_cols), \(x) x == "flapping")),
    n_gliding = rowSums(across(all_of(state_cols), \(x) x == "gliding")),

    # the number of methods that agree on the most common state
    n_agree = pmax(n_ascending, n_flapping, n_gliding),

    agreement = case_when(n_agree == 4 ~ "all 4 agree",
                          n_agree == 3 ~ "3 of 4 agree",
                          n_agree == 2 ~ "no majority"),

    # the state that at least 3 of the 4 methods agree on
    consensus = case_when(n_ascending >= 3 ~ "ascending",
                          n_flapping >= 3 ~ "flapping",
                          n_gliding >= 3 ~ "gliding",
                          TRUE ~ "no majority"),

    # when 3 of the 4 methods agree, which method disagrees?
    odd_one_out = case_when(n_agree != 3 ~ NA,
                            kmeans_inst != consensus ~ method_labels["kmeans_inst"],
                            kmeans_agg != consensus ~ method_labels["kmeans_agg"],
                            kmeans_comb != consensus ~ method_labels["kmeans_comb"],
                            hmm != consensus ~ method_labels["hmm"])
    ) %>%
  # set the order of the levels for plotting
  mutate(agreement = factor(agreement, levels = names(agreement_colours)),
         consensus = factor(consensus, levels = names(consensus_colours)),
         odd_one_out = factor(odd_one_out, levels = method_labels))


We also create a ‘long’ version of the data, with one row for each fix and method, which is easier to plot.


Show code
eagle_states_long <- eagle_states %>%
  select(stepstart_dtime, all_of(state_cols), n_ascending, n_flapping, n_gliding) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(state_cols), names_to = "method", values_to = "state") %>%
  mutate(method = factor(method_labels[method], levels = method_labels),
         # how many of the OTHER three methods agree with this method's state
         n_others_agree = case_when(state == "ascending" ~ n_ascending - 1,
                                    state == "flapping" ~ n_flapping - 1,
                                    state == "gliding" ~ n_gliding - 1))

title: Wedge-tailed eagle behavioural classification
section: Agreement between each pair of methods
text:
Agreement between each pair of methods
The percentage of fixes where each pair of methods classified the same state, and Cohen’s kappa, which accounts for the agreement that would be expected by chance given how often each method classifies each state (1 = perfect agreement, 0 = no better than chance).


Show code
# all pairs of methods
method_pairs <- combn(state_cols, 2, simplify = FALSE)

pairwise_agreement <- map(method_pairs, \(pair) {

  state_a <- eagle_states[[pair[1]]]
  state_b <- eagle_states[[pair[2]]]

  # proportion of fixes where both methods classified the same state
  p_observed <- mean(state_a == state_b)
  # agreement expected by chance, from the proportions of each state in each method
  p_chance <- sum(prop.table(table(state_a)) * prop.table(table(state_b)))

  tibble(method_a = method_labels[pair[1]],
         method_b = method_labels[pair[2]],
         agreement = p_observed,
         kappa = (p_observed - p_chance) / (1 - p_chance))

}) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(method_a = factor(method_a, levels = method_labels),
         method_b = factor(method_b, levels = method_labels))

title: Wedge-tailed eagle behavioural classification
text:
Create aggregated features
For each location (the focal fix) we summarise the flight variables over a centred moving window that extends half_window_s seconds before and after it, within the same flight segment. As the data are classified after the fact, a centred window avoids shifting the detected transitions later in time (as a backward-only window would). Windows are based on time rather than a number of fixes, as the fix-intervals vary (mostly 3–5 s).
Within each window we calculate:

turn_cum - the cumulative signed turning angle (radians). When thermalling the turns all have the same sign, so the sum grows steadily (roughly 2π per circle), whereas the GPS jitter of a perched or slow bird has a random sign and largely cancels out.
speed_mean - the mean ground speed (m/s, from F_Sn).
Vrate_mean - the mean signed vertical rate (m/s, from F_Vrate), i.e. the net climb or descent.
straightness - the net displacement across the window divided by the path length (0 = returning to the start, 1 = perfectly straight). This separates directional flight from circling, and complements turn_cum for perched/slow birds (low straightness but little net turning).
n_fixes - the number of fixes in the window. This is not for clustering, but shows where windows are truncated at the start and end of flight segments (or across gaps in the data).

The turning angle is taken from step_ta, which is in radians. The turning angle of the first fix of each flight segment is relative to a step outside that segment, so it is set to 0.
The windows are calculated after removing the extreme vertical rates (so they don’t contaminate the window means), but before the low-speed rows are dropped below. Where fixes are missing, straightness uses the straight line between the remaining fixes. Each column gets a _window suffix (e.g. F_turn_cum_window). The column names don’t depend on the window width, so half_window_s can be changed below and the rest of the notebook re-run without any other changes.


Show code
# half-width of the window in seconds (the window covers this many seconds
# before AND after the focal fix)
half_window_s <- 15

# sum of x across each window, using cumulative sums (fast on millions of rows).
# lo and hi are the indices of the first and last fixes in each window
window_sum <- function(x, lo, hi) {
  cs <- c(0, cumsum(x))
  cs[hi + 1] - cs[lo]
}

add_window_features <- function(data, half_window_s) {

  data %>%
    arrange(name, flight_n, stepend_dtime) %>%
    group_by(name, flight_n) %>%
    mutate(
      t = as.numeric(stepend_dtime),
      # first and last fixes within +/- half_window_s of each focal fix
      lo = findInterval(t - half_window_s, t, left.open = TRUE) + 1,
      hi = findInterval(t + half_window_s, t),
      n_fixes = hi - lo + 1,
      # turning angle (radians), ignoring the turn at the start of each flight segment
      ta = if_else(row_number() == 1, 0, step_ta),
      turn_cum = window_sum(ta, lo, hi),
      speed_mean = window_sum(F_Sn, lo, hi) / n_fixes,
      Vrate_mean = window_sum(F_Vrate, lo, hi) / n_fixes,
      # net displacement / path length, both from the positions of the fixes in the
      # window (so it stays <= 1 even when fixes have been filtered out). seg is the
      # distance from the previous fix, so the path in a window is the sum of
      # seg over fixes lo+1 to hi
      seg = c(0, sqrt(diff(stepend_utme)^2 + diff(stepend_utmn)^2)),
      path_length = window_sum(seg, lo, hi) - seg[lo],
      displacement = sqrt((stepend_utme[hi] - stepend_utme[lo])^2 +
                            (stepend_utmn[hi] - stepend_utmn[lo])^2),
      straightness = if_else(path_length > 0, displacement / path_length, 0),
      .after = F_radians_abs
    ) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(-c(t, lo, hi, ta, seg, path_length, displacement)) %>%
    rename_with(\(x) paste0("F_", x, "_window"),
                c(turn_cum, speed_mean, Vrate_mean, straightness)) %>%
    rename_with(\(x) paste0(x, "_window"), n_fixes)

}

eagle_data <- add_window_features(eagle_data, half_window_s)

title: Wedge-tailed eagle behavioural classification
text:
Smooth the behaviours
To avoid abrupt and unrealistic changes in behaviour, Scacco et al. (2019) reassigned any segment with a different behaviour from its neighbours to the most common behaviour of the two segments before and after it. We do the same here, but for the fixes within each flight segment. Any fix with a different behaviour from both the previous and the next fix is reassigned to the most common behaviour of the smooth_n fixes before and after it (if there is a tie, it takes the behaviour of the previous fix). The first and last fixes of each flight segment are not changed.
As our variables are already calculated over a moving window, this only changes a small proportion of the fixes, but it removes most of the single-fix ‘blips’ in behaviour. Increasing smooth_n considers more neighbours, but still only changes the fixes that differ from both of their immediate neighbours. The unsmoothed behaviours are kept in the behavior_unsmoothed column.


Show code
# number of fixes either side to consider (Scacco et al. used two segments either side)
smooth_n <- 2

eagle_data <- eagle_data %>%
  arrange(name, flight_n, stepend_dtime) %>%
  group_by(name, flight_n) %>%
  mutate(
    # is the behaviour different from both the previous and the next fix?
    # (this is NA for the first and last fixes of each flight segment, so set those to FALSE)
    isolated = behavior_unsmoothed != lag(behavior_unsmoothed) &
      behavior_unsmoothed != lead(behavior_unsmoothed),
    isolated = replace_na(isolated, FALSE),
    # indices of the first and last fixes within smooth_n fixes of each fix
    i = row_number(),
    lo = pmax(i - smooth_n, 1),
    hi = pmin(i + smooth_n, n()),
    # number of neighbouring fixes with each behaviour (subtracting the focal fix itself),
    # using the window_sum function from above
    n_ascending = window_sum(behavior_unsmoothed == "ascending", lo, hi) - (behavior_unsmoothed == "ascending"),
    n_flapping = window_sum(behavior_unsmoothed == "flapping", lo, hi) - (behavior_unsmoothed == "flapping"),
    n_gliding = window_sum(behavior_unsmoothed == "gliding", lo, hi) - (behavior_unsmoothed == "gliding"),
    # the most common behaviour of the neighbours (or the previous fix's behaviour if there's a tie)
    neighbour_mode = case_when(
      n_ascending > n_flapping & n_ascending > n_gliding ~ "ascending",
      n_flapping > n_ascending & n_flapping > n_gliding ~ "flapping",
      n_gliding > n_ascending & n_gliding > n_flapping ~ "gliding",
      TRUE ~ lag(behavior_unsmoothed)
      ),
    # replace the behaviour of the isolated fixes
    behavior = if_else(isolated, neighbour_mode, behavior_unsmoothed)
    ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # remove the columns that were only needed for the smoothing
  select(-c(isolated, i, lo, hi, n_ascending, n_flapping, n_gliding, neighbour_mode)) %>%
  # reorder the levels
  mutate(behavior = factor(behavior, levels = c("ascending", "flapping", "gliding")))

title: Wedge-tailed eagle behavioural classification
text:
Create aggregated features
For each location (the focal fix) we summarise the flight variables over a centred moving window that extends half_window_s seconds before and after it, within the same flight segment. As the data are classified after the fact, a centred window avoids shifting the detected transitions later in time (as a backward-only window would). Windows are based on time rather than a number of fixes, as the fix-intervals vary (mostly 3–5 s).
Within each window we calculate:

turn_cum - the cumulative signed turning angle (radians). When thermalling the turns all have the same sign, so the sum grows steadily (roughly 2π per circle), whereas the GPS jitter of a perched or slow bird has a random sign and largely cancels out.
speed_mean - the mean ground speed (m/s, from F_Sn).
Vrate_mean - the mean signed vertical rate (m/s, from F_Vrate), i.e. the net climb or descent.
straightness - the net displacement across the window divided by the path length (0 = returning to the start, 1 = perfectly straight). This separates directional flight from circling, and complements turn_cum for perched/slow birds (low straightness but little net turning).
n_fixes - the number of fixes in the window. This is not for clustering, but shows where windows are truncated at the start and end of flight segments (or across gaps in the data).

The turning angle is taken from step_ta, which is in radians. The turning angle of the first fix of each flight segment is relative to a step outside that segment, so it is set to 0.
The windows are calculated after removing the extreme vertical rates (so they don’t contaminate the window means), but before the low-speed rows are dropped below. Where fixes are missing, straightness uses the straight line between the remaining fixes. Each column gets a _window suffix with the half-width (e.g. F_turn_cum_window).


Show code
# half-width of the window in seconds (the window covers this many seconds
# before AND after the focal fix)
half_window_s <- 15

# sum of x across each window, using cumulative sums (fast on millions of rows).
# lo and hi are the indices of the first and last fixes in each window
window_sum <- function(x, lo, hi) {
  cs <- c(0, cumsum(x))
  cs[hi + 1] - cs[lo]
}

# also get the standard deviation within the window
window_sd <- function(x, lo, hi) {
  n   <- hi - lo + 1
  cs  <- c(0, cumsum(x))
  cs2 <- c(0, cumsum(x^2))

  s  <- cs[hi + 1]  - cs[lo]    # sum of x in window
  s2 <- cs2[hi + 1] - cs2[lo]   # sum of x^2 in window

  v <- (s2 - s^2 / n) / (n - 1)
  sqrt(pmax(v, 0))              # guard against tiny negative values from rounding
}

# run the function across the data
add_window_features <- function(data, half_window_s) {

  data %>%
    arrange(name, flight_n, stepend_dtime) %>%
    group_by(name, flight_n) %>%
    mutate(
      t = as.numeric(stepend_dtime),
      # first and last fixes within +/- half_window_s of each focal fix
      lo = findInterval(t - half_window_s, t, left.open = TRUE) + 1,
      hi = findInterval(t + half_window_s, t),
      n_fixes = hi - lo + 1,
      # turning angle (radians), ignoring the turn at the start of each flight segment
      ta = if_else(row_number() == 1, 0, step_ta),
      turn_cum = window_sum(ta, lo, hi),
      speed_mean = window_sum(F_Sn, lo, hi) / n_fixes,
      speed_sd = window_sd(F_Sn, lo, hi),
      Vrate_mean = window_sum(F_Vrate, lo, hi) / n_fixes,
      Vrate_sd = window_sd(F_Vrate, lo, hi),
      # net displacement / path length, both from the positions of the fixes in the
      # window (so it stays <= 1 even when fixes have been filtered out). seg is the
      # distance from the previous fix, so the path in a window is the sum of
      # seg over fixes lo+1 to hi
      seg = c(0, sqrt(diff(stepend_utme)^2 + diff(stepend_utmn)^2)),
      path_length = window_sum(seg, lo, hi) - seg[lo],
      displacement = sqrt((stepend_utme[hi] - stepend_utme[lo])^2 +
                            (stepend_utmn[hi] - stepend_utmn[lo])^2),
      straightness = if_else(path_length > 0, displacement / path_length, 0),
      .after = F_radians_abs
    ) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(-c(t, lo, hi, ta, seg)) %>% #, path_length, displacement
    rename_with(\(x) paste0("F_", x, "_window"),
                c(turn_cum, speed_mean, speed_sd, Vrate_mean, Vrate_sd, 
                  path_length, displacement, straightness)) %>%
    rename_with(\(x) paste0(x, "_window"), n_fixes)

}

title: Wedge-tailed eagle behavioural classification
text:
State-dependent distributions
Each variable needs a distribution that matches its range and shape (see the histograms above):









Variable
Description
Range
Distribution in hmmTMB




F_radians_abs
Absolute turning angle (radians)
0 to \(\pi\)
Beta ("beta"), on F_radians_abs / pi


F_Sn
Speed (step length / time, m/s)
> 0, right-skewed
Gamma ("gamma2"), with mean and sd parameters


F_Vrate
Vertical rate (m/s)
Negative and positive
Normal ("norm")



Turning angles are usually modelled with a circular distribution (e.g. von Mises or wrapped Cauchy). Here we use the absolute turning angle because the eagles circle in both directions. It lies between 0 (straight ahead) and \(\pi\) (a complete reversal), so we divide it by \(\pi\) to put it on the 0–1 scale and use a beta distribution. The beta distribution is flexible: it can have most of its values close to 0 (straight flight), or be spread across the range (circling).
For speed we use the gamma2 distribution, which is a gamma distribution parameterised by its mean and standard deviation (rather than shape and rate). This makes the initial values easier to choose.
The gaps in the vertical rate histogram are likely because altitude is recorded to the nearest metre and divided by fix intervals of 3–5 s, so only some values are possible. The normal distribution is an approximation, but should be adequate for separating climbing, level and descending flight.
Other assumptions to keep in mind:

Each flight segment (flight_n) is a separate time series, so the model doesn’t link the end of one flight to the start of the next.
HMMs assume a regular time interval between observations. Most fix intervals are 4 s (with some 3 s and 5 s), and some rows were removed above (extreme vertical rates and speeds < 1 m/s), leaving small gaps. As speed and vertical rate are both per second, we treat the fixes as regular here.

title: Wedge-tailed eagle behavioural classification
text:
Prepare the data


Show code
# hmmTMB treats each level of an 'ID' column as a separate time series, and the
# rows of each ID must be together and in time order. We sort eagle_data itself
# (rather than just the copy for hmmTMB), so that the decoded states can be
# added straight back onto it in the same row order
eagle_data <- eagle_data %>%
  arrange(name, flight_n, stepend_dtime) %>%
  # drop flights with only a single fix. There are no transitions to learn from,
  # and hmmTMB's state decoding fails for a time series with one observation
  group_by(name, flight_n) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

# update ready_to_cluster so that it still lines up with eagle_data (it's used
# for the PCA below)
ready_to_cluster <- eagle_data %>% select(all_of(clustering_variables))

hmm_data <- eagle_data %>%
  mutate(
    # one time series per flight segment. The eagle's name is included so that the
    # IDs stay unique when using all eagles. fct_inorder() keeps the factor levels in
    # the same order as the rows, which some hmmTMB functions (e.g. state_probs())
    # rely on - alphabetical levels would mismatch them
    ID = fct_inorder(paste(name, flight_n, sep = "_")),
    # absolute turning angle as a proportion of pi (0 = straight ahead, 1 = a
    # complete reversal)
    F_turn_prop = F_radians_abs / pi,
    # the beta distribution doesn't include exactly 0 or 1, so nudge any values
    # at the boundaries slightly inside
    F_turn_prop = pmin(pmax(F_turn_prop, 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6)
  ) %>%
  # the turning angle at the first fix of each flight is relative to a step
  # outside the flight, so set it to NA. hmmTMB allows missing values - that fix
  # is still used, but only through its speed and vertical rate
  group_by(ID) %>%
  mutate(F_turn_prop = if_else(row_number() == 1, NA, F_turn_prop)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # keep only the columns that we need, as a plain data frame
  select(ID, F_turn_prop, F_Sn, F_Vrate) %>%
  as.data.frame()

text:
Model set-up


Show code
# the distribution for each variable (names must match the columns of hmm_data)
dists <- list(
  F_turn_prop = "beta",  # absolute turning angle / pi
  F_Sn = "gamma2",       # speed (m/s) - gamma distribution with a mean and sd
  F_Vrate = "norm"       # vertical rate (m/s)
)

# The beta distribution's parameters (shape1 and shape2) aren't intuitive, so this
# helper converts a mean and sd of the absolute turning angle in radians into the
# shape parameters (on the 0-1 scale). It only works when sd < sqrt(mean * (pi - mean))
beta_shapes <- function(mean, sd) {
  m <- mean / pi  # mean on the 0-1 scale
  s <- sd / pi    # sd on the 0-1 scale
  nu <- m * (1 - m) / s^2 - 1
  list(shape1 = m * nu,
       shape2 = (1 - m) * nu)
}

# e.g. a state with a mean absolute turning angle of 0.25 radians (sd = 0.25)
beta_shapes(mean = 0.25, sd = 0.25)


$shape1
[1] 0.8408451

$shape2
[1] 9.725526



Initial values
The parameters are estimated by numerical optimisation, which starts from initial values for every parameter. Poor initial values can cause the optimiser to get stuck at a local maximum of the likelihood, or fail to converge (Glennie et al. 2023). We choose initial values that reflect the behaviours we expect, informed by the histograms and the k-means clusters. They also set the order of the states (state 1, state 2, etc). They are only starting points, and the model estimates the final values.
The initial values below were checked by refitting the models from random starting values (see Check for local maxima). For three and four states, the values were also adjusted to be close to the estimated values, to keep the state order consistent across the models (e.g. the circling state is always the last state). The state names in the comments are only hypotheses - check the estimated distributions and the flight paths before naming the states.
The models take a few minutes each to fit with Stella’s data (~500,000 fixes).

# state 1: straight, fast and descending (e.g. gliding and directional flight)
# state 2: turning, slower and climbing (e.g. thermal soaring)

  F_turn_prop = beta_shapes(mean = c(0.25, 1),  # radians
                            sd   = c(0.25, 0.8)),
  F_Sn = list(mean = c(13, 9),                  # m/s
              sd   = c(3.5, 4)),
  F_Vrate = list(mean = c(-1, 0.7),             # m/s
                 sd   = c(1.5, 1))

# single initial state distribution for all flights. The default ("estimated")
# estimates a separate one for every flight, which adds thousands of parameters

# combine them into a hidden Markov model and estimate the parameters

hmm2$fit(silent = TRUE)

title: Wedge-tailed eagle behavioural classification
text:
Check for local maxima
The optimiser can converge to a local maximum rather than the global maximum, which becomes more likely with more states. A simple check is to refit a model from several random starting values and compare the log-likelihoods. If none of the random starts reach a higher log-likelihood than our model, we can be more confident that it is the global maximum. The states may come out in a different order from random starts, but the log-likelihood is the same when the solution is the same.
This chunk is not run when rendering (eval: false) as it refits the model several times, but it can be run interactively. Change n_states to check the other models.


Show code
n_states <- 3   # the model to check
n_tries <- 5    # the number of random starting values

llk_tries <- rep(NA, n_tries)

set.seed(1)

for(i in 1:n_tries) {

  # random initial values for each state, within plausible ranges
  turn_means <- runif(n_states, 0.1, 2)  # radians
  par0_random <- list(
    F_turn_prop = beta_shapes(mean = turn_means, sd = 0.6 * turn_means),
    F_Sn = list(mean = runif(n_states, 5, 16),
                sd = runif(n_states, 2, 4)),
    F_Vrate = list(mean = runif(n_states, -2.5, 1.5),
                   sd = runif(n_states, 0.8, 1.5))
  )

  hid_try <- MarkovChain$new(data = hmm_data, n_states = n_states, initial_state = "shared")
  obs_try <- Observation$new(data = hmm_data, dists = dists, n_states = n_states, par = par0_random)
  hmm_try <- HMM$new(obs = obs_try, hid = hid_try)
  hmm_try$fit(silent = TRUE)

  llk_tries[i] <- hmm_try$llk()

}

# log-likelihoods from the random starts, compared to the model fitted above
llk_tries
list(hmm2, hmm3, hmm4)[[n_states - 1]]$llk()

Model comparison
AIC and BIC (lower is better) always favour more states when there is this much data, as extra states also soak up structure that the model doesn’t include (such as autocorrelation or differences between flights), rather than finding distinct behaviours (Pohle et al. 2017). The number of states should therefore be chosen mainly on whether the states are biologically interpretable, and on the model checks below.

# parameters that the optimiser actually estimated

                   "3 states" = hmm3,
                   "4 states" = hmm4)

  model = names(hmm_models),
  log_lik = map_dbl(hmm_models, \(m) m$llk()),
  n_par = map_dbl(hmm_models, \(m) length(m$out()$par))
) %>%
  mutate(
    AIC = -2 * log_lik + 2 * n_par,
    BIC = -2 * log_lik + log(nrow(hmm_data)) * n_par,
    delta_AIC = AIC - min(AIC),
    delta_BIC = BIC - min(BIC)
  )

title: Wedge-tailed eagle behavioural classification
text:
Create aggregated features
For each location (the focal fix) we summarise the flight variables over a centred moving window that extends half_window_s seconds before and after it, within the same flight segment. As the data are classified after the fact, a centred window avoids shifting the detected transitions later in time (as a backward-only window would). Windows are based on time rather than a number of fixes, as the fix-intervals vary (mostly 3–5 s).
Within each window we calculate:

turn_cum - the cumulative signed turning angle (radians). When thermalling the turns all have the same sign, so the sum grows steadily (roughly 2π per circle), whereas the GPS jitter of a perched or slow bird has a random sign and largely cancels out.
speed_mean - the mean ground speed (m/s, from F_Sn).
Vrate_mean - the mean signed vertical rate (m/s, from F_Vrate), i.e. the net climb or descent.
straightness - the net displacement across the window divided by the path length (0 = returning to the start, 1 = perfectly straight). This separates directional flight from circling, and complements turn_cum for perched/slow birds (low straightness but little net turning).
n_fixes - the number of fixes in the window. This is not for clustering, but shows where windows are truncated at the start and end of flight segments (or across gaps in the data).

The turning angle is taken from step_ta, which is in radians. The turning angle of the first fix of each flight segment is relative to a step outside that segment, so it is set to 0.
The windows are calculated after removing the extreme vertical rates (so they don’t contaminate the window means), but before the low-speed rows are dropped below. Where fixes are missing, straightness uses the straight line between the remaining fixes. Each column gets a _window suffix with the half-width (e.g. F_turn_cum_window).


Show code
# half-width of the window in seconds (the window covers this many seconds
# before AND after the focal fix)
half_window_s <- 15

# sum of x across each window, using cumulative sums (fast on millions of rows).
# lo and hi are the indices of the first and last fixes in each window
window_sum <- function(x, lo, hi) {
  cs <- c(0, cumsum(x))
  cs[hi + 1] - cs[lo]
}

# also get the standard deviation within the window
window_sd <- function(x, lo, hi) {
  n   <- hi - lo + 1
  cs  <- c(0, cumsum(x))
  cs2 <- c(0, cumsum(x^2))

  s  <- cs[hi + 1]  - cs[lo]    # sum of x in window
  s2 <- cs2[hi + 1] - cs2[lo]   # sum of x^2 in window

  v <- (s2 - s^2 / n) / (n - 1)
  sqrt(pmax(v, 0))              # guard against tiny negative values from rounding
}

# run the function across the data
add_window_features <- function(data, half_window_s) {

  data %>%
    arrange(name, flight_n, stepend_dtime) %>%
    group_by(name, flight_n) %>%
    mutate(
      t = as.numeric(stepend_dtime),
      # first and last fixes within +/- half_window_s of each focal fix
      lo = findInterval(t - half_window_s, t, left.open = TRUE) + 1,
      hi = findInterval(t + half_window_s, t),
      n_fixes = hi - lo + 1,
      # turning angle (radians), ignoring the turn at the start of each flight segment
      ta = if_else(row_number() == 1, 0, step_ta),
      turn_cum = window_sum(ta, lo, hi),
      speed_mean = window_sum(F_Sn, lo, hi) / n_fixes,
      speed_sd = window_sd(F_Sn, lo, hi),
      Vrate_mean = window_sum(F_Vrate, lo, hi) / n_fixes,
      Vrate_sd = window_sd(F_Vrate, lo, hi),
      # net displacement / path length, both from the positions of the fixes in the
      # window (so it stays <= 1 even when fixes have been filtered out). seg is the
      # distance from the previous fix, so the path in a window is the sum of
      # seg over fixes lo+1 to hi
      seg = c(0, sqrt(diff(stepend_utme)^2 + diff(stepend_utmn)^2)),
      path_length = window_sum(seg, lo, hi) - seg[lo],
      displacement = sqrt((stepend_utme[hi] - stepend_utme[lo])^2 +
                            (stepend_utmn[hi] - stepend_utmn[lo])^2),
      straightness = if_else(path_length > 0, displacement / path_length, 0),
      .after = F_radians_abs
    ) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(-c(t, lo, hi, ta, seg)) %>% #, path_length, displacement
    rename_with(\(x) paste0("F_", x, "_window"),
                c(turn_cum, speed_mean, speed_sd, Vrate_mean, Vrate_sd, 
                  path_length, displacement, straightness)) %>%
    rename_with(\(x) paste0(x, "_window"), n_fixes)

}

title: Wedge-tailed eagle energy harvesting
section: Calculate the agreement between the methods
text:
Calculate the agreement between the methods
For each fix we count how many of the four methods classified it as each state. From this we get:

n_agree - the number of methods that agree on the most common state (2, 3 or 4)
agreement - whether all 4 methods agree, 3 of the 4 agree, or there is no majority (a 2-2 or 2-1-1 split)
consensus - the state that at least 3 of the 4 methods agree on (otherwise ‘no majority’)
odd_one_out - when 3 of the 4 methods agree, the method that disagrees



Show code
eagle_states <- eagle_states %>%
  mutate(
    # the number of methods that classified each fix as each state
    n_ascending = rowSums(across(all_of(state_cols), \(x) x == "ascending")),
    n_flapping = rowSums(across(all_of(state_cols), \(x) x == "flapping")),
    n_gliding = rowSums(across(all_of(state_cols), \(x) x == "gliding")),

    # the number of methods that agree on the most common state
    n_agree = pmax(n_ascending, n_flapping, n_gliding),

    agreement = case_when(n_agree == 4 ~ "all 4 agree",
                          n_agree == 3 ~ "3 of 4 agree",
                          n_agree == 2 ~ "no majority"),

    # the state that at least 3 of the 4 methods agree on
    consensus = case_when(n_ascending >= 3 ~ "ascending",
                          n_flapping >= 3 ~ "flapping",
                          n_gliding >= 3 ~ "gliding",
                          TRUE ~ "no majority"),

    # when 3 of the 4 methods agree, which method disagrees?
    odd_one_out = case_when(n_agree != 3 ~ NA,
                            kmeans_inst != consensus ~ method_labels["kmeans_inst"],
                            kmeans_agg != consensus ~ method_labels["kmeans_agg"],
                            kmeans_comb != consensus ~ method_labels["kmeans_comb"],
                            hmm != consensus ~ method_labels["hmm"])
    ) %>%
  # set the order of the levels for plotting
  mutate(agreement = factor(agreement, levels = names(agreement_colours)),
         consensus = factor(consensus, levels = names(consensus_colours)),
         odd_one_out = factor(odd_one_out, levels = method_labels))

title: Wedge-tailed eagle energy harvesting
section: Pull out just the ascending state (soaring)
text:
Pull out just the ascending state (soaring)
We keep only the fixes that at least 3 of the 4 methods classified as ascending, and then split them into separate soaring bouts.
For each soaring fix we calculate the gap between the end of the previous soaring step and the start of this one, which is the time that the eagle spent doing something else (gliding, flapping, or a fix with no majority). Consecutive soaring steps have a gap of 0 seconds. A new bout starts when:

the gap is longer than max_gap_s (60 seconds), or
(optional, currently commented out) the soaring fix is in a different flight segment to the previous one. Flight segments are separated by gaps in the data of at least ~30 seconds (where the eagle may have landed), so this stops a bout continuing across them even when the gap is less than 60 seconds. Uncomment the flight_n != lag(flight_n) line to add this condition.

Short interruptions (e.g. a few fixes of gliding between thermals, or a misclassified fix) therefore stay within the same bout.
Bouts that are shorter than min_bout_s (60 seconds) are removed in the next section, as these are often only a few fixes (sometimes just one) and are more likely to be brief climbs or misclassifications than thermal or slope soaring.


Show code
soaring_locations <- eagle_states %>% filter(consensus == "ascending")

# the longest gap (in seconds) between soaring fixes within the same bout
max_gap_s <- 60

# the shortest bout (in seconds) to keep - shorter bouts are removed below
min_bout_s <- 60

# split soaring into bouts if there are gaps more than max_gap_s seconds
soaring_locations <- soaring_locations %>%
  # put the fixes in time order for each eagle
  arrange(name, stepstart_dtime) %>%
  group_by(name) %>%
  mutate(
    # time (s) between the end of the previous soaring step and the start of this one
    gap_s = as.numeric(difftime(stepstart_dtime, lag(stepend_dtime), units = "secs")),
    # TRUE when this fix starts a new bout - the first soaring fix of each eagle
    # (where gap_s is NA), after a long gap, or in a new flight segment
    new_bout = is.na(gap_s) |
      gap_s > max_gap_s, # |
      # flight_n != lag(flight_n),
    # number the bouts for each eagle (cumsum counts up by 1 at every new bout)
    bout_n = cumsum(new_bout)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # a unique id for each bout (in case there are multiple eagles)
  mutate(bout_id = paste(name, bout_n, sep = "_"))

title: Wedge-tailed eagle energy harvesting
text:
Summarise each soaring bout
For each bout we calculate:

duration_s - the time from the start of the first soaring step to the end of the last soaring step (including any short gaps)
soaring_s - the time spent soaring (the sum of the soaring step durations, so excluding the gaps)
alt_gain_m - the altitude gained while soaring (vertical rate × step duration, summed over the soaring steps)
mean_Vrate - the mean vertical rate (m/s) of the soaring fixes

We then remove the bouts with a duration_s shorter than min_bout_s, and the soaring fixes from those bouts, so that everything below only uses the bouts that are at least 60 seconds long.


Show code
soaring_bouts <- soaring_locations %>%
  # duration of each step (s)
  mutate(step_s = as.numeric(difftime(stepend_dtime, stepstart_dtime, units = "secs"))) %>%
  # (bout_n before bout_id, so the bouts stay in time order)
  group_by(name, bout_n, bout_id) %>%
  summarise(
    flight_n = first(flight_n),
    start = min(stepstart_dtime),
    end = max(stepend_dtime),
    n_fixes = n(),
    duration_s = as.numeric(difftime(end, start, units = "secs")),
    soaring_s = sum(step_s),
    alt_gain_m = sum(F_Vrate * step_s),
    mean_Vrate = mean(F_Vrate),
    # the centre of the bout (in UTM for ggplot and lat/lon for leaflet)
    utme = mean(stepend_utme),
    utmn = mean(stepend_utmn),
    lat = mean(lat),
    lon = mean(lon),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Time spent soaring
The total time spent soaring (in bouts of at least min_bout_s), compared to the total flight time (the sum of the step durations of all of the fixes that were classified by all four methods).

title: Wedge-tailed eagle energy harvesting
text:
Spatial layers
We read in the spatial layers and crop them to the area around the soaring locations (plus a buffer), so they are quick to plot. Add any other rasters to raster_files to include them in the leaflet map below - the names are used as the layer names in the map.
The rasters are at 30 m resolution. If the soaring locations cover a large area (e.g. when using all eagles), uncomment the aggregate() line to use a coarser resolution, otherwise the maps will be slow and the leaflet map may hit its size limit.


Show code
# the spatial layers to crop (and add to the leaflet map)
raster_files <- c(elevation = "mapping/HS_DEM.tif",
                  tpi_300m = "mapping/TPI_300m.tif",
                  slope = "mapping/HS_Slope.tif",
                  ruggedness = "mapping/HS_Ruggedness.tif",
                  aspect = "mapping/Aspect_degrees.tif")

# the area to crop to - the extent of the soaring locations plus a buffer (m)
buffer_m <- 2000

crop_area <- ext(min(soaring_locations$stepend_utme) - buffer_m,
                 max(soaring_locations$stepend_utme) + buffer_m,
                 min(soaring_locations$stepend_utmn) - buffer_m,
                 max(soaring_locations$stepend_utmn) + buffer_m) %>%
  # the eagle locations are in GDA94 / MGA zone 55
  vect(crs = "EPSG:28355")

# read in and crop each raster (the crop area is projected to the crs of each
# raster, in case some are in a different crs)
spatial_layers <- map(raster_files, \(f) {
  r <- rast(f)
  r <- crop(r, project(crop_area, crs(r)))
  # r <- aggregate(r, fact = 5) # 5 x 5 cells, i.e. 150 m resolution
  r
})

title: Wedge-tailed eagle energy harvesting
text:
Interactive map
The centre of each soaring bout over a satellite (or topographic) basemap, coloured by the altitude gained in that bout. Hover over a bout to see its details. The spatial layers are added as overlays that can be switched on in the layer control (top right) - they are hidden when the map loads.


Show code
# colour palette for the altitude gained in each bout
bout_palette <- colorNumeric("viridis", domain = soaring_bouts$alt_gain_m)

# hover labels for each bout
bout_labels <- paste0("<b>", soaring_bouts$bout_id, "</b><br>",
                      format(soaring_bouts$start_local, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"), "<br>",
                      "Duration: ", round(soaring_bouts$duration_s / 60, 1), " min<br>",
                      "Altitude gained: ", round(soaring_bouts$alt_gain_m), " m<br>",
                      "Mean vertical rate: ", round(soaring_bouts$mean_Vrate, 2), " m/s") %>%
  map(htmltools::HTML)

# basemaps
soaring_map <- leaflet(soaring_bouts, height = 650, width = "100%",
                       options = leafletOptions(preferCanvas = TRUE)) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.WorldImagery, group = "Satellite") %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$OpenTopoMap, group = "Topographic")

# add each spatial layer (in greyscale, so the bouts stand out), with its own legend
for (layer in names(spatial_layers)) {

  r <- spatial_layers[[layer]]
  layer_palette <- colorNumeric("Greys", domain = range(values(r), na.rm = TRUE),
                                na.color = "transparent", reverse = TRUE)

  soaring_map <- soaring_map %>%
    addRasterImage(r, colors = layer_palette, opacity = 0.8, group = layer) %>%
    addLegend(position = "bottomleft", pal = layer_palette,
              values = range(values(r), na.rm = TRUE), title = layer, group = layer)
}

soaring_map %>%
  addCircleMarkers(lng = ~lon, lat = ~lat, radius = 4, stroke = FALSE,
                   fillColor = ~bout_palette(alt_gain_m), fillOpacity = 0.9,
                   label = bout_labels, group = "Soaring bouts") %>%
  addLegend(position = "bottomright", pal = bout_palette, values = ~alt_gain_m,
            title = "Altitude gained (m)", group = "Soaring bouts") %>%
  addLayersControl(baseGroups = c("Satellite", "Topographic"),
                   overlayGroups = c(names(spatial_layers), "Soaring bouts"),
                   options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)) %>%
  # hide the spatial layers when the map loads
  hideGroup(names(spatial_layers)) %>%
  addScaleBar(position = "bottomleft")

text:
Prevalence of soaring
There are multiple different ways that we could associate climbing behaviour with landscape variables to predict where wedge-tailed eagles are harvesting environmental energy.

Presence of soaring (positive vertical rate) in that cell
Occurrence of soaring (presence of uplifts) and flapping flight (absence of uplifts) (as per Scacco et al. (2019))
Proportion of time spent soaring in that cell, compared to the total proportion of time spent in that cell
Average positive vertical rate (of the soaring behaviour only)
Maximum positive vertical rate (of the soaring behaviour only)
